stem: Which of the following is the formula for What a Logarithm Is — Laws, Special Values, Domain?
candidateDistractors: \(\log_a M = \log_a N \Rightarrow M = N,\ \text{then require } M,N > 0\)
trapHints: \(\log(M+N)\) is NOT \(\log M + \log N\): The product law splits a log of a product, not a log of a sum. \(\log_a(M+N)\) has no simplification — only \(\log_a(MN)\) splits into \(\log_a M+\log_a N\).

The base must be \(>0\) and \(\neq 1\): \(\log_a N\) is only defined for a base \(a > 0,\ a \neq 1\). A base of \(1\) is forbidden because \(1^x = 1\) for every \(x\), so \(\log_1 N\) has no unique value; a base \(\le 0\) breaks the exponential entirely.

stem: Which of the following is the formula for Change of Base & the Reciprocal Identity?
trapHints: Reciprocal flips the base and the argument together: \(\dfrac{1}{\log_a b} = \log_b a\) — the base and argument swap. It does NOT equal \(\log_a(1/b)\) (which would be \(-\log_a b\)). Keep the two operations separate.

Change of base does NOT invert the fraction: \(\log_b a = \dfrac{\log a}{\log b}\) — the NEW argument \(a\) goes on top, the NEW base \(b\) on the bottom. Writing it upside-down as \(\dfrac{\log b}{\log a}\) gives \(\log_a b\), the reciprocal, and flips the whole answer.

trapHints: An algebraic root is not a solution until the domain clears it: \(x-1 = (x-3)^2\) gives \(x = 2\) and \(x = 5\), but \(x = 2\) makes \(x-3 = -1 < 0\), so \(\log_2(x-3)\) is undefined. Only \(x = 5\) is a genuine solution — always re-substitute into the ORIGINAL equation.

The argument must be strictly positive — \(0\) is not allowed: \(\log_a x\) is undefined for \(x \le 0\), and that includes \(x = 0\): there is no power of \(a\) that gives \(0\). A root that makes ANY argument equal to \(0\) (not just negative) must be rejected — the domain requires every argument \(> 0\), strictly.
